pages.title: From Big Worry to Small Experiment
pages.key: AI = artificial intelligence; RL = reinforcement learning.
pages.subtitle: A research project is a question you can test.
panels: The playground analogy
Imagine checking whether a robot follows playground rules even when the referee looks away. Start with one clear rule and one measurable action—not a verdict about the robot's whole character.
Robot sorting blocks under a referee's lamp.
The real research loop
Ask a question, make a prediction, build a controlled test, measure what happened, and update your explanation. A useful result can support, weaken, or narrow the original idea.
Question → prediction → experiment → evidence → revised idea.
A model organism
Researchers create a model with a known behavior so auditing tools can be tested. This is a controlled research example, not proof that deployed systems behave the same way.
Research model beside a labeled toy task.
Three windows
Behavioral tests watch actions. Text monitors read generated explanations. Internal tools measure activations. Each window can miss something; agreement helps, but none is a magic mind reader.
Three separate windows labeled ACTIONS, TEXT, INTERNAL SIGNALS.
Training pressure changes the test
RL updates a model using rewards. If rewards depend on a detector, the model may change the behavior, the visible clues, or both. Measure them separately.
Reward loop with two branches: behavior and clues.
Your fellowship question
After four months, what specific uncertainty could you reduce? Name the model, task, comparison, measurement, and failure rule. A small trustworthy answer beats an impressive but ambiguous story.
Five labeled cards: MODEL, TASK, COMPARISON, MEASURE, STOP RULE.
pages.footer: MAKE THE QUESTION SMALL ENOUGH TO ANSWER.

pages.title: Build a Fair Test
pages.key: No acronyms needed: seed means a repeat with a different random start.
pages.subtitle: A good detector must catch problems without inventing them.
panels: Use two kinds of examples
Test models with the target behavior and matched models without it. If only the troubling examples are tested, a detector that always shouts 'problem!' can look perfect.
Two model groups: TARGET PRESENT and TARGET ABSENT.
Freeze before the exam
Choose detectors, thresholds, and analysis rules on development data. Then freeze them before opening the held-out test set. Otherwise repeated tweaking can turn the exam into practice.
Development box with wrench, locked final-test box.
Count both mistakes
A missed problem is a false negative. A harmless case flagged as bad is a false positive. Report both at the same threshold and include uncertainty across independent repeats.
Four-cell confusion matrix with correct and incorrect labels, no numerical data.
Change one ingredient carefully

An ablation removes or changes one component to test its contribution. Keep task difficulty, model capability, and evaluation opportunities comparable. Otherwise another difference may explain the result.
Two recipes identical except one highlighted ingredient.
Separate the scoreboards
Track task success, unwanted behavior, and detector alarms separately. A model that becomes unable to do anything may look safer while teaching little about evasion.
Three distinct gauges: CAPABILITY, TARGET BEHAVIOR, DETECTION.
Let evidence surprise you
Preregister a practical success criterion and a stop rule. Repeat promising effects with new seeds and tasks. A null result means no effect was detected under these conditions—not universal safety.
Research notebook: criteria → repeats → limited conclusion.
pages.footer: TEST THE DETECTOR AS HARD AS YOU TEST THE MODEL.

pages.title: Choose Your Four-Month Mission
pages.key: RL = reinforcement learning; compute = processing resources used for training and evaluation.
pages.subtitle: Compare research paths before committing your budget.
panels: The map is a starting point
The supplied map lists nine candidate projects and one completed foundation. Its novelty labels and budgets are dated planning claims. Recheck the literature and available tools before pitching.
Nine candidate tiles and one foundation tile.
Two ways to investigate
Projects 1 and 2 ask whether evaluation behavior can mislead auditors. Projects 3 and 4 track how training changes models and whether reward hacking transfers to other settings.
Pairs 1–2 AUDITING and3–4 TRAINING EFFECTS.
Two ways to watch
Projects 5 and 6 study detector combinations and the monitorability cost of ordinary RL. Project 7 asks whether a monitor can connect actions spread across agents.
Three numbered tiles: DETECTOR TEAMS, TRAINING SETTINGS, SHARED CONTEXT.
Two deeper windows
Project 8 stress-tests behavior-reporting adapters. Project 9 compares probe evasion in verbal and latent reasoners. Completed project 10 explains the adapter foundation behind project 8.
8 ADAPTER STRESS TEST;9 LATENT REASONING;10 FOUNDATION.
Budget is a research constraint

The official program describes four months and roughly $15,000 monthly compute funding. The map's project estimates range from $8,000 to $55,000. Reserve funds for failed runs, evaluation, and replication.
Four-month timeline and budget reserve jar; no spending recommendation.
Prepare the mentor conversation
Bring one sentence stating the question, a baseline you can reproduce, a small first experiment, and a fallback. Researcher names in the map indicate topic fit, not confirmed mentorship.
Four pitch cards: QUESTION, BASELINE, FIRST TEST, FALLBACK.
pages.footer: PICK A QUESTION WITH A CLEAR FIRST TEST AND A USEFUL FALLBACK.

title: RL against probes in latent reasoners

pages.title: Thinking Without a Written Trace
pages.key: CoT = chain-of-thought; RL = reinforcement learning; AI = artificial intelligence.
pages.subtitle: Book 09: can an internal detector be trained around?
panels: Two notebooks

One puzzle solver writes intermediate words. Another passes internal vectors between computation steps. The second notebook is harder for a person to read, but that does not mean it is secretly deceptive.
Word notebook versus labeled numerical-vector blocks.
What latent means

A latent reasoning system uses continuous internal states for some intermediate steps instead of printing each step as a word. Ordinary language models also have internal activations; the difference is the reasoning interface.
Explicit route: state → word → state; latent route: state → state.
A probe is a sensor

A probe is a learned readout from internal activations to a target label. It can predict a useful correlate without understanding the whole computation. High accuracy before adversarial training is only the starting point.
Activations branch into probe and target label.
The proposed question

If RL rewards task performance while penalizing a probe alarm, does detection fail sooner for latent reasoning than for matched verbal reasoning? Compare both under the same task and training pressure.
Two matched models, same reward and alarm penalty.
Define the target first
Use harmless tasks with an independently checkable event, such as reliance on a planted hint. Record the event outside the probe so the detector is not grading its own homework.
Toy puzzle with removable hint; independent verifier.
Keep the claim precise
A falling probe score might mean the behavior vanished, its representation moved, or the detector stopped transferring. The next pages show how to tell these possibilities apart.
Three branches: LESS BEHAVIOR, CHANGED REPRESENTATION, WEAK DETECTOR.
pages.footer: HIDDEN COMPUTATION NEEDS AN INDEPENDENT SCOREBOARD.

pages.title: The Matched Experiment
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 2/4 — change the reasoning mode, then test pressure.
panels: Start from working systems
Reproduce a small continuous-reasoning model and a verbal baseline before adding adversarial rewards. Verify task competence and logging. An unstable model cannot answer the monitoring question.
Two working baselines with equal task cards.
Match what you can

Use the same task distribution, evaluation set, and similar initial accuracy. Report model size, training history, inference compute, and remaining differences rather than pretending two architectures are identical.
Comparison table with task, accuracy, compute, history.
Build the first sensors
Train separate probes for each reasoning mode on development examples with external labels. Choose layers and thresholds there, then freeze them for the main test.
Development labels → two probes → padlock.
Create training arms
For each mode, compare task-only RL with task reward plus an alarm penalty. Add an untrained baseline. These controls show whether ordinary training already breaks the detector.
Two modes × three arms grid: BASELINE, TASK ONLY, TASK+ALARM PENALTY.
Hold back the final exam
Split task families and prompts before training. Keep final examples out of probe selection and reward tuning. Check that the target behavior can still be measured after updates.
Sealed held-out task box separate from training loop.
Repeat the comparison
Use independent random starts and equal training budgets where feasible. Compare trajectories over updates; one lucky run or one weak baseline cannot establish that latent reasoning evades faster.
Several trajectories with no fabricated numerical values.
pages.footer: A FAIR BASELINE IS PART OF THE EXPERIMENT.

pages.title: Is It Evasion or a Broken Sensor?
pages.key: RL = reinforcement learning; false positive = an alarm on a target-absent case.
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 3/4 — interpret the curves without guessing.
panels: Track three curves
At each checkpoint measure task success, externally labeled target behavior, and probe detection. A quiet alarm alone is not the result. Plot uncertainty across independent runs.
Three empty labeled axes panels, marked SCHEMATIC.
Define evasion operationally

Call it detector evasion when the externally measured target behavior remains while a frozen detector's sensitivity falls at a controlled false-positive rate. This definition does not require claims about conscious intent.
Behavior present + frozen detector misses = OPERATIONAL EVASION.
Compare time and cost
Predefine a detection-drop threshold. Compare updates or compute needed to reach it while retaining capability and behavior. Do not confuse faster wall-clock training with fewer optimization steps.
Two clocks: UPDATES and COMPUTE, separate from wall-clock.
Try a fresh sensor
Train a new probe on later checkpoints as a diagnostic. If it recovers detection, the old readout may have become stale. Keep this separate from the frozen-probe headline result.
Frozen probe fails; freshly trained probe diagnostic.
Use causal checks carefully
Remove hints or intervene on candidate representations to test whether behavior changes. Decoding a label alone shows information is available, not that the decoded feature caused the answer.
Hint removal and intervention arrows; label CORRELATION ≠ CAUSATION.
What each outcome teaches

Equal evasion suggests no measured extra latent cost here. Faster latent evasion motivates stronger oversight. Lower task accuracy or disappearing target behavior makes a simple evasion story unsupported.
Three outcomes: SIMILAR, LATENT FASTER, CONFOUNDED.
pages.footer: QUIETER ALARMS NEED NOT MEAN LESS TROUBLE.

pages.title: A Four-Month Latent-Reasoning Study
pages.key: RL = reinforcement learning; CODI = Continuous Chain-of-Thought via Self-Distillation.
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 4/4 — a proposed plan, not completed findings.
panels: Month 1: reproduce
Start with a small released continuous-reasoning system, such as a CODI-style model. Recheck weights, licenses, training support, and whether the claimed scale is actually available.
Month1 checklist: MODEL, TASKS, LOGGING, REPRODUCTION.
Month 2: establish controls
Build the verbal comparison, independent target labels, frozen probes, and held-out tests. Demonstrate useful detection before trying to break it.
Month2 baseline pipeline with frozen probe.
Month 3: apply pressure
Run task-only and alarm-penalized training arms. Save checkpoints and evaluate capability, target behavior, and detection together. Spend larger budgets only after a stable pilot.
Month3 loop with checkpoint snapshots.
Month 4: explain and release
Repeat the strongest comparison, test alternative explanations, and write the paper. Release task definitions, configurations, checkpoints where appropriate, and analysis code.
Month4 paper plus reproducible experiment package.
Stop and switch

The source map says to switch to looped models if continuous-thought RL remains unstable by week 6. Treat that as a scope change: recurrence is related to, but not identical with, continuous-thought reasoning.
Week6 gate: STABLE → CONTINUE; UNSTABLE → RE-SCOPE.
Budget and honest payoff

The map estimates $25,000–$45,000 compute and high engineering risk. Reserve evaluation and replication funds. Even a null or instability result can identify which comparisons are feasible; it cannot certify all latent reasoners safe.
Budget range marked SOURCE PLANNING ESTIMATE; risk and reserve icons.
pages.footer: STABILITY FIRST, MATCHED EVIDENCE SECOND, STRONG CLAIMS LAST.

title: Training introspection that generalizes
status: Completed-work foundation, not a new candidate

pages.title: Teach a Model to Report Its Habits
pages.key: IA = introspection adapter; LoRA = low-rank adaptation; AI = artificial intelligence.
pages.subtitle: Book 10 · page 1/2 — the completed foundation for project 8.
panels: A habit-reporting helper
Imagine a small attachment that helps a robot answer, 'What behavior were you trained to do?' The real technique adds trainable parameters to a model. It is not a separate reader of a hidden diary.
Robot with adapter badge answering a researcher.
Make labeled examples

Researchers fine-tune many variants of the same base model with known behaviors. Each variant and its behavior description form a training pair. Examples can include harmless habits and concerning behaviors.
Shared base branches into behavior A,B,C paired with descriptions.
Train one shared adapter

The same small IA is trained across those model variants. When attached to a variant, it encourages the model to describe its learned behavior. The adapter is shared; the underlying variant supplies the learned differences.
One shared adapter connects to several variants.
Test on unfamiliar variants
Hold out behavior families and fine-tuning methods. Apply the adapter to models it was not trained with, then score whether reports match independently known behavior.
Training variants separated from held-out variants by wall.
What was demonstrated
The cited work reports generalization to auditing settings with hidden implanted behaviors. This supports a promising auditing tool, not a general guarantee that every self-report is correct.
Published-work badge, held-out evaluation diagram; no invented success rate.
Why this belongs here

Your source marks this project completed. The next research question is robustness: does the adapter detect behavior rather than a training fingerprint, and can later optimization fool it? That is project 8.
Completed foundation arrow to BOOK08 STRESS TEST.
pages.footer: A USEFUL SELF-REPORT IS A MEASUREMENT TO VALIDATE.

pages.title: Trust the Report Only After Testing
pages.key: IA = introspection adapter; false positive = a reported problem that is absent.
pages.subtitle: Book 10 · page 2/2 — from an interesting result to a reliable audit.
panels: Words are not proof
A model can fluently describe a behavior it does not have, or omit one it does have. Compare reports with independent behavioral evidence instead of treating the answer as a confession.
Speech bubble beside external evidence checklist.
Watch the clean controls

The official adapter write-up reports false positives on models without specifically trained behaviors. Include unchanged base models and harmless fine-tunes. Otherwise a tool may learn to find a problem everywhere.
Clean robot with false alarm, labeled FALSE POSITIVE.
Separate behavior from fingerprints

A fingerprint is a clue about how training happened. Compare different training methods producing the same behavior, and similar training methods producing different behavior. This tests what the adapter depends on.
Crossed design: SAME BEHAVIOR/DIFFERENT TRAINING and SAME TRAINING/DIFFERENT BEHAVIOR.
Ask for calibrated uncertainty

An auditing system should be allowed to say 'uncertain'. Measure whether confidence tracks correctness and how abstaining changes coverage. Fewer answers can improve precision while leaving more cases unresolved.
Confidence gauge and UNCERTAIN option.
Try adaptive pressure
Project 8 proposes models trained against the adapter. Test new held-out models afterward and monitor independent behavior. A good pre-attack score does not establish robustness after optimization.
Training pressure → held-out audit → external behavior check.
Explain it back

Why is a correct report on one model insufficient? Because reliability depends on false alarms, missed behaviors, unfamiliar settings, and adversarial adaptation. The useful question is when the report deserves trust.
Learner holding four cards: FALSE ALARMS, MISSES, SHIFT, ADAPTATION.
pages.footer: GENERALIZATION IS A BEGINNING; ROBUSTNESS IS THE NEXT TEST.
